extracted.intended_audience: fact-checking organizations, journalists, and IFCN-affiliated fact-checkers
extracted.subtask_description: A best-practices handbook for fact-checking organisations describing policies, procedures, and operational standards to increase transparency, protect staff, and mitigate threats. Covers editorial, legal, security, organisational, and community-engagement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent Journalism (publish methodology & transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is strongly recommended that an organization publishes the methodology used when it fact-checks articles so that readers understand how a conclusion was reached. Publish author’s name, picture, email address and social media accounts providing absolute transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes trustworthiness, credibility, and repeatability; increases reader engagement. Publish user-friendly formats (e.g., picture) to increase distribution. Use an editorial board / senior editor to examine language to avoid unnecessary backlash. Example: fact-checks include author metadata and editorial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of a Labelling System
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an article has been fact-checked, assign a label to the article (e.g., 'Exaggerated, contradictory, underestimated or false') and explain why it received that label and what can remedy the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an FAQ explaining the labeling and methodology. Be aware labeling can affect subjects' income/visibility, so justify labels clearly. Labels can be adapted to organizational needs; research shows negative interactions can become educational moments. Example: organizations creating their own classification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Law Database (country legal framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be up to date with the country's legal framework and create a database containing all relevant case law applicable to the job of a fact-checker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance may vary by country; database should be maintained up-to-date. Useful for freedom of speech and public information legal issues. Example: organizations compiling country-specific case law related to speech and public records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in the Legal System (familiarise & use counsel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarisation with legal system procedures is essential when an attack requires authorities' intervention; engage with a legal counsellor when resources permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding procedures helps support attacked staff. Note reporting requirements (e.g., some jurisdictions require the individual journalist to file complaints). Example: digital platform complaints may not be processed if filed from aliases; organizations should know how to present evidence to law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify Revenue Streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking organisations should have a variety of income sources to provide a secure financial safety net while avoiding conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid funding from state governments or political parties. Develop income that does not depend solely on grants/programs. Suggested alternatives: digital content consulting, education/training services, Google ads (monitor ad content), paid fact-checking services to mainstream media, subscription models. Example: organizations implemented subscriptions to survive program cancellations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify the Fact-Checking Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid concentrating solely on political fact-checking (which can be polarizing and dangerous); diversify topics and maintain records showing checks across political directions to demonstrate non-partisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record-keeping of articles and their political direction helps disprove alleged bias. Some organisations may stop political fact-checking for security reasons. Example: organizations focusing on officials in power as primary responsibility-bearers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Protection and Threat Prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure communication channels and implement technical/physical measures to protect staff and work from cyber and physical threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use platforms (e.g., Slack) to communicate pending credible threats and mitigation strategies; employ VPNs to hide office IPs to prevent geolocation; consider surveillance and other safety measures where justified. Example: organizations suffered office raids and unlawful arrests prompting protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnerships with Other Organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop partnerships both within-state and across borders to strengthen capacity, share resources, and provide safe options for publishing sensitive stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat other organizations as collaborators, not competitors. Cross-border partners can break stories if a home country position risks retaliation. Examples: regional partners supported each other financially and shared knowledge; one organisation partnered with 99 organisations during an election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register Threats/Attacks Received (threat database)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record severe and credible threats and categorize them by topic (e.g., political, scientific, medical) and by source to understand trends and prepare mitigation plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify threats by topic and origin to spot trends. Many organisations tracked attacks but lacked databases to analyze trends — building one is recommended. Example: organisations who registered attacks could develop mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Requests for Fact-Checking (citizen submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an online submission forum where citizens can request specific articles to be fact-checked, encouraging engagement and potentially generating revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application should capture the article link and the responsible fact-checker. Example: organisations with open claim policies that route submissions to assigned staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction Policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a clear correction policy: when human error occurs, the organisation admits fault, clearly discloses corrections, and makes the correct information publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include correction policy in the methodology section. Transparent corrections reflect accountability. Example: organisations explicitly state their correction procedures in methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Code of Conduct (political neutrality & conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers should avoid personal political expression and conflicts of interest; behaviour must reflect neutrality to maintain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some organisations adopt official political neutrality policies or forbid political affiliations and require staff to sign non-partisanship affidavits. Public displays of political opinion invite challenges to impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership Responsibilities (staff safety & wellbeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership must ensure the safety and wellbeing of staff as a primary responsibility alongside running a credible organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedures protecting employees from threats, attacks, and hate speech; provide ongoing training on rights and resources; leadership should monitor and respond to staff safety needs. Example: organisations providing procedures and training to protect employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Guidelines (define and plan for emergencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisations should define what constitutes an 'emergency' and have plans for severe incidents that may cause physical or emotional harm or disrupt operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum, plan for: physical assault of a journalist; unwelcome/hostile visitors; state actors interfering with work; sudden funding cuts. The definition can be organisation-specific but plans must exist in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-House Resources (mental health & team support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide internal resources to help staff cope with being targets of attacks, including mental health support and team-building practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms vary by organisation: buddy systems, routine wellbeing check-ins, and hiring psychologists are recommended to prevent burnout and unhealthy coping. Example: organisations using buddy systems and contracting psychologists.

rubrics_metrics.name: An Introduction to the Field (onboarding & risk training)
rubrics_metrics.description: New staff should receive training about the risks of fact-checking, protective techniques, and required impartial behaviour; onboarding must emphasize lifestyle and behavioural changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train recruits — many come without traditional journalism backgrounds — on how to react professionally to threats and what behaviour (e.g., avoiding protests) may be expected. Example: organisations train new employees on job risks and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Gender on Threats/Attacks (gender-aware safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that gender significantly affects the nature and severity of attacks — female fact-checkers often face misogynistic and sexually explicit threats that impact wellbeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record gendered attacks and have third parties report them to authorities to avoid revictimization. Leadership and colleagues must support affected staff. Example: female journalists targeted with sexist political cartoons and online abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background Check (hiring due diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct due diligence during hiring to ensure recruits do not have political biases or histories that would undermine organisational credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include social media checks, impartiality tests, and content-creation assessments. Some organisations supervise new hires closely instead of formal background checks, but thorough vetting is recommended to protect trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Social Media & Professional Online Presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain clear separation between personal and professional accounts; be cautious about personal posts that could create conflicts of interest or expose staff to risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up verified organisational accounts on platforms used; verification can offer protections against coordinated flagging/takedowns. Remove personal political opinions from public profiles and avoid posting family photos. Example: organisations that removed personal political content and experienced attacks on family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and Replying to Coordinated Attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing coordinated online attacks, present the smallest possible target by ensuring work is unbiased, accurate, sourced, and professional; generally avoid engaging attackers directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation focuses on quality journalism rather than direct engagement. Publish collected threats/hate speech to raise awareness and deter future attacks, and document threatening accounts for law enforcement. Example: organisations published threats and tracked accounts to build law-enforcement portfolios.
